I. "The quality of mercy" is a speech given by Portia in William Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (Act 4, Scene 1).
In the speech, Portia, disguised as a lawyer, begs Shylock to show mercy to Antonio. The speech extols the power of
mercy, "an attribute to God Himself."
The quality of mercy is not strain'd.
It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven
Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest:
It blesseth him that gives and him that takes.
'Tis mightiest in the mightiest; it becomes
The thronéd monarch better than his crown.
His scepter shows the force of temporal power,
The attribute to awe and majesty
Wherein doth sit the dread and fear of kings;
But mercy is above this sceptered sway.
It is enthroned in the hearts of kings;
It is an attribute to God Himself;
And earthly power doth then show likest God's
When mercy seasons justice. Therefore, Jew,
Though justice be thy plea, consider this:
That in the course of justice none of us
Should see salvation. We do pray for mercy,
And that same prayer doth teach us all to render
The deeds of mercy. I have spoke thus much
To mitigate the justice of thy plea,
Which, if thou follow, this strict court of Venice
Must needs give sentence 'gainst the merchant there.
Source: Portia, in William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act 4, Scene 1.

II. The Gujarat High Court recently mandated the expedited installation of CCTV cameras in the Registry in a strategic
manner to prevent any tampering with court documents. This decision came after an incident where it was discovered that
someone had intentionally interfered with the listing of a case on the ‘admission board’ of a judge. The judge observed
that this was a clear attempt to obstruct the administration of justice and emphasized that such activities, especially in the
Registry of the state's highest court, cannot be tolerated. The court highlighted the lack of comprehensive CCTV coverage
in the Registry, which hindered the collection of conclusive evidence in this particular case.
The incident in question involved a practicing advocate, who, along with others in his circle, was known for engaging in
such practices, particularly in the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT). The advocate had filed a petition in 2020 to quash a
case against him, where he was initially booked for demanding a bribe while acting as a court-appointed commissioner for
the DRT Ahmedabad.
The judge had previously indicated reluctance to consider the advocate's plea and had directed the Bar Council of Gujarat
to initiate proceedings against the lawyer for professional misconduct. The case was listed on the ‘admission board’ but
was later found to have been tampered with and posted as item number 200 in the ‘final hearing board,’ a tactic to avoid a
hearing since the court typically hears cases up to item number 70 in the daily list.
In 2016, the then Chief Justice of the High Court had approved the installation of CCTVs in all judicial departments of the
Registry to ensure the safety of judicial proceedings. However, despite specific approval and the urgency of the matter,
there had been no progress in installing the cameras. The court expressed concern over this delay and ordered the
Registrar General, along with the Registrar (Vigilance) and (Judicial), to coordinate with the additional secretary of the
Chief Justice to expedite the process of installing CCTVs in every corner of the Registry and, if necessary, in the
courtrooms as well. This task was directed to be completed by January 15, 2024.
The court's decision underscores the importance of transparency and security in judicial proceedings and the need for
effective measures to prevent any interference with the administration of justice.

IV. A recent scientific observation revealed that Mars' atmosphere underwent a significant expansion due to an unusual
solar wind event. This incident was recorded when a spacecraft in orbit around Mars detected a stark change in the
Martian atmosphere on a specific date in December 2022. The expansion of Mars' magnetosphere and ionosphere was so
extensive that it resulted in a tripling of its size. This dramatic change was caused by a void created by an intense gust of
solar wind.
This type of phenomenon is not entirely unprecedented. A similar incident occurred in the late 1990s when Earth's
magnetosphere experienced a substantial outward swelling, caused by a sudden decrease in solar wind, leading to a
dramatic increase in its volume. These occurrences provide a rare glimpse into the dynamics of planetary interactions with
their surrounding environments in the solar system, especially under varying solar conditions.
The study's lead researcher expressed initial scepticism upon witnessing the drastic reduction in solar wind and the
consequent atmospheric changes. The research has shed light on Mars’ response to unusual solar system conditions,
offering valuable insights.
Solar wind, a continuous flow of particles from the Sun, exerts a consistent pressure throughout the solar system,
diminishing at a boundary known as the heliopause. The event on Mars, however, involved an atypical scenario where two
solar winds interacted: a slower wind was overtaken by a faster one, resulting in a combined, more powerful 'superwind.'
The spacecraft recorded an increased particle density in this merged solar wind. Subsequently, a notable decrease in
particle density was observed, indicating an uncommonly low-density and weak solar wind.
This unique situation has provided researchers with an opportunity to study Mars in a different light, particularly how it
would react if it orbited a star with a less intense solar wind. Understanding these interactions is vital for comprehending
the complex dynamics of our solar system. It also holds significance for future explorations and studies of Mars and other
celestial bodies.
The research findings are being presented at a major scientific meeting, contributing significantly to our understanding of
Mars and its interactions with solar wind phenomena. This study enhances our knowledge of planetary science and the
behaviours of celestial bodies under varying cosmic conditions.

II. The law of torts is a collection of all the circumstances in which court gives a remedy by way of damages, for legally
unjustified harm or injury done by one to another person. There are three elements which need to be proved before
constituting a tort:
    There must be an act or omission on the part of the defendant.
    That act or omission should be in violation of a legal right vested in the plaintiff.
    The wrongful act or omission thus done by the defendant is of such a nature to give rise to a legal remedy.
Damnum sine Injuria refers to damages without injury or damages where no legal right of the plaintiff is infringed. The
principle is that if one exercises his rights, without infringing another’s legal right, it doesn't give rise to an action in tort.
An example cited is the case of Mayor & Co. of Bradford vs. Pickles (1895), where the defendant's act of digging a well
cut the water supply to the corporations well. The court ruled in favour of the defendant as no legal right was violated.
In the case of Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd vs. McGregor, Gow & Co. is cited, the plaintiff, an independent ship-owner,
suffered losses due to the actions of defendant ship-owners. The court ruled that the defendants acted within the law, even
if it caused harm to the plaintiff.
Injuria sine damno is a violation of a legal right without causing harm or damage. Whenever a legal right is infringed, the
person in whom the right is vested can take action. An example is Ashby Vs. White (1703), where the plaintiff, a voter, was
wrongfully denied his vote by the defendant, a returning officer. Even though the candidate he wished to vote for won, the
defendants were held liable for infringing on the plaintiff's legal right.
In the case of Bhim Singh vs. State of Jammu & Kashmir, Bhim Singh, an MLA, was arrested and prevented from
attending a legislative assembly session. The court ruled in his favor, stating a violation of his rights under Articles 21 &
22 of the Constitution.
Damnum Sine Injuria pertains to moral wrongs without legal remedies, while Injuria Sine Damnum concerns legal wrongs
that are actionable even without actual loss. The former emphasizes actions within legal bounds that may cause harm,
while the latter focuses on the violation of legal rights.

Revocation is the act of annulment. Section 5 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, stipulates that a contract can be revoked
any time before the communication of acceptance is made to the proposer. Once acceptance is communicated, the contract
cannot be revoked. Section 6 lays down the methods by which a revocation of a proposal can be made, and this article
elaborates on these methodologies prescribed by the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
One method is the revocation of a proposal by communication of notice, where a proposal may be revoked by the
proposer by giving notice to the offeree before it is accepted. Another method is revocation by lapse of time. If there is a
time period prescribed for acceptance, the proposal gets revoked if the acceptance is not communicated before the expiry
of the prescribed time period.
A proposal can also be revoked if the condition precedent to acceptance is not fulfilled. If the offeree fails to comply with
certain conditions before acceptance of the proposal, the proposal can revoke the offer. Death or insanity of the proposer is
another method by which a proposal can be revoked, if the fact of his death or insanity comes into the knowledge of the
offeree before the communication of acceptance.
Other methods include rejection of the proposal, death of the offeree, making a counter offer, acceptance not being made
in the mode prescribed, subsequent illegality or destruction of the subject matter of a proposal. For instance, a proposal is
revoked if a counter offer is made to it, and the acceptance of the counter offer amounts to rejection of the original offer.
Contracts are considered closed when the acceptance is communicated, and revocation has an overriding effect over the
accepted principles of communication of proposal and acceptance of proposal. The courts sometimes interfere in such
cases by modifying the contract between the parties, but it is not their duty to make the contracts for the parties. The
interpretation of law involved often leads to courts being asked to examine the validity of the revocation of a proposal,
